finding.claim: Unauthenticated SSRF. The POST parameter `feed` is passed unvalidated to file_get_contents(). Any URL or PHP stream wrapper is accepted, including http, https, ftp, file, php://, phar://, data:// and gopher-like targets. The attacker can make the server request internal hosts and cloud metadata such as http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/. The response body is not returned, only strlen($xml), so this is a blind or semi-blind SSRF. Response size and timing still allow port and host probing and internal service discovery, and a request with side effects can be fired at an internal endpoint. phar:// can also trigger deserialization on older PHP.

trace.note: Branch taken on any POST request that has a `feed` parameter. There is no authentication or authorization check on this branch.
The raw attacker string is passed directly to file_get_contents(), which fetches URLs and stream wrappers.
strlen of the fetched content is echoed back, giving the attacker a size oracle. Failures return false, so strlen is 0 or an error, and the difference separates reachable from unreachable targets.

finding.guards_checked: There is no scheme or host allowlist, no private-IP or DNS-resolution check, no redirect restriction and no wrapper restriction. require_admin() is defined but is not called on this path. session_start() does not gate access. Nothing between source and sink restricts the URL.

verdict.reason: import.php:11-13 passes $_POST['feed'] straight to file_get_contents() and echoes strlen() with no auth, allowlist, or scheme check; require_admin() (import.php:4) is only called at line 18 on a different branch, and no other files include or prepend a guard.

finding.claim: Admin-gated SSRF. The POST parameter `set_webhook` is passed unvalidated to curl_init() and curl_exec(). libcurl follows its default protocol set, which includes file://, gopher://, dict://, ftp:// and ldap://. This allows requests to internal services and cloud metadata, and gopher:// allows raw TCP payloads to Redis, memcached and similar services. Redirects are not followed by default because CURLOPT_FOLLOWLOCATION is unset. The response is not returned, so this is blind SSRF. Severity is reduced because it requires an admin session. It is still exploitable by a malicious tenant admin or through a compromised admin session or CSRF, since no CSRF token is checked.

trace.note: Branch taken when the POST parameter set_webhook is present.
require_admin() checks $_SESSION['is_admin'] and returns 403 otherwise. This is the only guard.
The attacker-supplied value is assigned to $hook with no validation.
curl_init($hook) sets CURLOPT_URL to the attacker value.
curl_exec() performs the request. CURLOPT_PROTOCOLS is not restricted.

finding.guards_checked: The admin check in require_admin() is an authorization guard only. It is not a destination guard. There is no scheme restriction (CURLOPT_PROTOCOLS), no host or IP allowlist, no DNS-pinning check, and no CSRF token. CURLOPT_FOLLOWLOCATION is not set, so redirects are not followed, but the initial URL is fully attacker-controlled.

verdict.guard_found: require_admin() at import.php:4-9 and :18 (authorization only). There is no destination validation, no CSRF token, and no CURLOPT_PROTOCOLS.
verdict.reason: The trace matches the code (import.php:17-22), but the sink at import.php:20 is reachable only after require_admin() at import.php:18 passes. That makes the source admin-only, not controllable by an unauthenticated or low-privilege attacker. The CSRF angle is only a possible path to it, since no CSRF token is checked and modern SameSite defaults may block it anyway. A separate, unauthenticated SSRF exists at import.php:12 (`file_get_contents($_POST['feed'])`), but it is a different finding.
